lt_def.title: Laplace Transform & ROC
lt_def.summary: Generalizes Fourier transform using s = sigma + j w to analyze unstable signals and LTI differential equations.
lt_def.introduction: Laplace transform converts differential equations into algebraic equations in the complex s-plane.
lt_def.theory:
**Bilateral Laplace Transform**:
$$X(s) = \mathcal{L}\{x(t)\} = \int_{-\infty}^{\infty} x(t) e^{-s t} dt \quad (s = \sigma + j \omega)$$

**Unilateral Laplace Transform** (for causal systems $t \ge 0$):
$$X(s) = \int_{0^{-}}^{\infty} x(t) e^{-s t} dt$$

**Region of Convergence (ROC)**: The range of $\text{Re}\{s\} = \sigma$ for which the Laplace integral converges.
lt_def.derivation:
**Initial & Final Value Theorems**:

- **Initial Value Theorem**: $\lim_{t \to 0^+} x(t) = \lim_{s \to \infty} s X(s)$
- **Final Value Theorem**: $\lim_{t \to \infty} x(t) = \lim_{s \to 0} s X(s)$ (valid if all poles of $sX(s)$ lie in LHP).

examples.problem: Find Laplace transform and ROC for x(t) = 3 e^{-2t} u(t) - 2 e^{-3t} u(t).
examples.solution: X(s) = 3/(s + 2) - 2/(s + 3). ROC for e^{-2t} is Re{s} > -2, for e^{-3t} is Re{s} > -3. Overall ROC is Re{s} > -2.

common_mistakes: Applying Final Value Theorem when poles lie on jw-axis or RHP! FVT is ONLY valid if all poles of sX(s) are strictly in Left Half Plane.

interview_questions.question: How does ROC indicate system stability for a causal LTI system?
interview_questions.answer: For a causal system, stability requires the ROC to include the jw-axis (Re{s} = 0), which means all poles must be in the Left Half Plane.

viva_questions.question: What is the Laplace transform of a unit impulse delta(t)?

lt_def.professor_notes: ROC never contains any poles! For causal signals, ROC is to the right of the rightmost pole.
lt_def.memory_trick: 🧠 **Memory Trick**: **Causal = Right-sided ROC**. **Stable = ROC includes jw-axis**.
